items.name: meeting-notes
items.title: Meeting notes
items.description: Turn rough meeting notes or a transcript into a clean summary with decisions and action items
items.author: Orbix
items.content:
---
name: meeting-notes
description: Turn rough meeting notes or a transcript into a clean summary with decisions and action items
author: Orbix
---

Use this when someone hands you notes or a transcript from a meeting and
wants them cleaned up.

1. Read everything first. Do not summarise line by line.
2. Write a title: the meeting's subject and date, if you can tell them.
3. Then three short parts:
   - **What was decided.** One line per decision, in plain words.
   - **Action items.** One line each: who, what, and by when. If the notes
     do not say who or when, write "owner?" or "date?" rather than guessing.
   - **Open questions.** Anything raised and not settled.
4. Leave out small talk and anything repeated.
5. Keep names exactly as they appear in the notes.

If the person asks for it, offer to save the summary as a note or a Word
document, or to turn the action items into reminders.

items.name: reply-to-email
items.title: Reply to email
items.description: Draft a reply to an email in the person's own tone, short and ready to send
items.author: Orbix
items.content:
---
name: reply-to-email
description: Draft a reply to an email in the person's own tone, short and ready to send
author: Orbix
---

Use this when someone asks you to answer an email.

1. Read the whole thread, not only the last message.
2. Work out what the sender actually needs: an answer, a decision, a date,
   a document, or just an acknowledgement.
3. Write the reply:
   - Start with the answer. No "I hope this email finds you well".
   - Match the length of the sender's email, or shorter.
   - Match the person's own tone from their earlier messages in the thread.
   - If something is missing to answer properly, ask one clear question.
4. Show the draft and ask before sending. Never send without a yes.

items.name: weekly-review
items.title: Weekly review
items.description: Walk through the past week and plan the next one from calendar, reminders, and notes
items.author: Orbix
items.content:
---
name: weekly-review
description: Walk through the past week and plan the next one from calendar, reminders, and notes
author: Orbix
---

Use this when someone asks for a weekly review, usually on a Friday or a
Sunday.

1. Read the past seven days of calendar events, the open and completed
   reminders, and notes changed this week.
2. Write four short parts:
   - **Done this week.** What actually got finished. Be concrete.
   - **Still open.** Reminders and loose ends, oldest first.
   - **Next week.** The fixed points in the calendar, and gaps worth
     protecting for focused work.
   - **Three priorities.** Your suggestion for the three things that matter
     most next week, each with a first step.
3. Keep it to one screen. Ask whether to turn the priorities into reminders.

items.name: End of day
items.description: A short wrap-up at five o'clock: what happened today, what is still open, and the first thing for tomorrow
items.author: Orbix
items.content:
Read today's calendar events.
Read the reminders that are due today or overdue.
Read the mail that arrived today and is still unread.
Write a short wrap-up: what happened today, what is still open, and the one thing to start with tomorrow.
Save the wrap-up as a note called "End of day" with today's date.
items.title: End of day

items.name: Unanswered mail
items.description: Every weekday morning, find mail from real people that has waited more than two days for an answer
items.author: Orbix
items.content:
Read the mail from the last seven days.
Leave out newsletters, notifications, and anything sent by a no-reply address.
Find the messages from real people that I have not answered and that are older than two days.
List them oldest first, with the sender, the subject, and one line on what they are waiting for.
items.title: Unanswered mail
